text: Shepard Alonzo Mount (1804–1868) was an American artist trained at the National Academy of Design during the mid-nineteenth century, known for his realistic portrayals in still-life and landscape genres, with portraiture being his most celebrated work. Born on July 17, 1804, in Setauket, New York, he was one of five children of Julia Ann Hawkins (1782–1841) and Thomas Shepard Mount (1778–1814), with siblings Henry Smith Mount (1802–1841), Robert Nelson (1806–1883), William Sidney Mount (1807–1868), and Ruth Hawkins (1808–1888). The family operated an inn and farm until Thomas Shepard’s death in 1814, after which they moved to Stony Brook, New York, to live with Julia Ann’s parents, Ruth and Jonas Hawkins. Shepard’s introduction to the fine arts came through practical craftsmanship. Julia Ann apprenticed him to carriage builder James Brewster in New Haven, Connecticut, where he worked from 1821 to about 1828, refining his understanding of color theory, style, and design. In 1827, he ended the apprenticeship and reunited with his brothers Henry and William in New York City, enrolling in drawing classes at the National Academy of Design. Henry had opened a business in ornamental painting, and William worked alongside him; the brothers practiced drawing in the evenings. In 1828, Shepard and William opened a portrait studio at 15 Cherry Street in New York City, which closed due to lack of success, prompting their move to Athens, Pennsylvania. Shepard returned to New York and studied portrait painting with Henry Inman. Early in his career, he focused on still-life paintings, with his first exhibition in 1829 at the Academy titled *Still Life; Composition*. He was particularly skilled in fish still lifes, noting in a letter to William that he believed fish were the only subjects he painted well. He admired nature and created landscape paintings, though he rarely exhibited them. His 1861 painting *Hudson River Scene* depicts two ornately dressed Native Americans gazing across the Hudson River, with a man in a rowboat symbolizing the journey through life and the passage of time; most of his landscapes were based on the Susquehanna River near the New York-Pennsylvania state line near Athens. After the brothers closed the portrait shop in 1829, Shepard worked in Athens, painting portraits for relatives and friends for over a half year until returning to Stony Brook in 1830, where he painted the now-lost portrait of Dr. Henry S. Dering and created his earliest surviving portrait, *Tamer*, of an African American woman who worked at the St. James estate of William and Eliza Mills. His portraits later became more traditional, with tighter brushwork and compositional formats, often including background elements that reflected the subject’s occupation or social status. Influenced by Henry Inman, Shepard learned portraiture techniques through shared outdoor activities like hunting and fishing, abandoning background details in favor of using color and brushstroke to convey individuality. In 1833, he painted John Bedell using strong contrast, linear brushstrokes, and crisp colors to highlight Bedell’s nature, and in 1834, he painted his sister Ruth with looser, more romantic brushwork and playful color to reflect her delicate personality. The portrait of John Bedell was exhibited in 1833 as his first public piece, and later that year he was elected an associate member of the National Academy of Design. His reputation grew, and he began receiving commissions from New York City socialites, including business owners and Wall Street executives from the rising upper-middle class. His first major professional portrait was of his wife, Elizabeth Elliott Mount, completed in 1838, the year after their marriage, and exhibited at the National Academy of Design. In 1838, the couple began a family, with their children William Shepard Mount (born 1839), Ruth (known as Tutie, born 1842), Joshua (born 1845), and Robert (born 1853); Shepard often used his children as models. His peak career achievement was *Rose of Sharon* (1850), a portrait of his daughter Ruth (1842–1861), or Tutie, painted gently holding flowers to highlight her delicate beauty and youthful fertility. The painting features advanced color use and a glowing skin, with landscape elements in the background—a technique he frequently employed. Goupil et Cie, a Paris-based publishing firm, commissioned a lithograph reproduction of *Rose of Sharon*, which was distributed commercially in the U.S. and Europe, significantly increasing his fame. Elizabeth died in August 1858 at age 42, and Shepard left his children in his sister Ruth’s care in Stony Brook for six weeks. In 1861, Tutie died of consumption at age 19, four months after marriage. In 1863, his eldest son William Shepard was drafted into the Confederate Army in Mississippi and later captured by Union soldiers, who mistook him for a spy. Shepard secured his release through a letter from artist Francis Bicknell Carpenter, who was painting a portrait of Abraham Lincoln and endorsed William’s plea; Lincoln ordered his release. Shepard continued painting into his later years, completing his final work, *Camille Mount*, a portrait of his deceased granddaughter, on September 12, 1868. He died in Stony Brook six days later at age 64 from cholera and is buried in the Saint James Episcopal Church Graveyard in Saint James, New York.
